fixes.explanation: David waited patiently, and the LORD inclined to him and heard his cry. Heard, friend. I yell at my oven timer all day and it has never once heard me. David's cry reached the LORD, and that's the whole point of the verse.

I get why ignored comes to mind, because waiting can feel that way. But David says something else: the LORD inclined to him and heard his cry. That's what the verse tells us about the waiting. David ended up heard.

Scolded would be a real plot twist, but the verse doesn't go there. David says the LORD inclined to him and heard his cry. No scolding is mentioned anywhere in it. After all that patient waiting, David was heard.

I see why you'd think David's still wobbling, because he talks about miry clay. But David says the LORD set his feet upon a rock and made his footsteps firm. Firm doesn't sound like slipping and sliding. So this one is false.

David says the LORD put a new song in his mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. Think about that. The LORD lifted him out of the pit, and a song is what gets put in his mouth. I can't carry a tune in a bucket.
That's right. David says, “Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD.” It comes right after the new song. David isn't the only one in view, because many will see.
This one is actually true. David says, “Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD.” It's right there at the end of verse 3. Many will see, and fear, and trust.

Hidden isn't what David says. He talks about proclaiming and declaring these wonders and plans, and he says they are more than he can count. His point is how many there are, not that they're hidden. That's a good problem to have.

David says, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened.” Burnt offerings and sin offerings, he says, God did not require. That's what he says in this verse. I think David is pointing us toward listening.

David doesn't say anything about every family. In this verse he says, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” Then he says his ears have been opened, and that God did not require burnt offerings and sin offerings.

When he must makes it sound like a chore, and that's not David's tone. He says, “I delight to do Your will, O my God…” He also says, “Your law is within my heart.” That's a lot more than doing it when you have to.

David says, “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly…” He goes on to say he does not seal his lips. I'd compare him to me holding up a fresh batch and yelling, but he's doing something much better than I am.
Doubts doesn't match this verse at all. David says, “I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly…” He adds that he does not seal his lips. Proclaiming is what he says he does.
Friends aren't what David says here. He says, “my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see.” I think he's talking about how heavy his own sins feel. He doesn't mention friends turning on him.

David doesn't ask for the chance to strike them down. He prays that those who seek his life be ashamed and confounded, and that those who wish him harm be repelled and humiliated. He's asking the LORD to deal with it. Striking them down isn't in his prayer.
David says, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” His prayer for the seekers is about joy. I like a prayer that asks for gladness.

That's right. David prays that those who love God's salvation will always say, “The LORD be magnified!” It's a prayer for the ones who love the LORD's salvation. I'd say that's a line worth repeating.

This one is actually true. David prays that those who love God's salvation will always say, “The LORD be magnified!” It's right there in verse 16. Those who love His salvation are the ones he prays will say it.
